_meta.source: The Guardian World Cup 2026 player guide

Czechia: Having squeezed in via the playoffs, Koubek’s well-drilled side have hopes of advancing from a middling group. Read the team guide here.
The spine of the side has plenty of experience, led by Soucek in midfield, while Schick scored 16 Bundesliga goals this season.
A serious lack of technical players, with the team relying too heavily on physicality, work rate, aggression and set pieces.

Everything the Guardian does – from in-depth and exhaustive guides like these to critical investigative reporting – is funded by the direct backing of readers who believe in independent journalism. If you don't already, please consider supporting us today.
Mexico: Playing in a third World Cup on home soil, El Tri are competitive and flexible but may struggle to meet fans’ high expectations. Read the team guide here.
Flexible tactics, a tight defensive unit and an approach based on intensity, aggressive pressing and quick transitions.
Pressure as co-hosts could affect even an experienced squad, while Aguirre’s pragmatic approach has drawn criticism.
South Africa: Bafana Bafana have emerged from a stagnant period after hosting in 2010 and held off Nigeria in qualifying. Read the team guide here.
International setup revitalised under Broos, knitted together by Mokoena in midfield, and built on well-drilled teamwork.
A squad mainly made up of domestic players lacks wider experience and will rely heavily on counterattacks to create chances.
Korea Republic: The Taegeuk Warriors went unbeaten to qualify for their 11th straight finals, but ambitions do not extend far beyond escaping their group. Read the team guide here.
With a robust core, the team has a great spirit and a proper talisman in former Premier League golden boot winner Son.
Uncertainty over ideal formation, with a late switch to 3-4-3 during qualifying, plus fears about form and fitness of key players.
Canada: Marsch has turned the co-hosts into a solid and settled team, and worked to develop the mentality to handle pressure. Read the team guide here.
Consistent 4-4-2 approach built on pressing from the front and pace out wide, all backed by a resilient defensive unit.
Fitness fears over star man Davies, a competitive group and the burden of never having won a World Cup match.
Qatar: The 2022 hosts stumbled through qualifying but could benefit from a much lower profile in these finals. Read the team guide here.
Hugely experienced coach Lopetegui will put hard focus on soaking up pressure and looking to hit opponents on the break.
Defence was a mess in qualifying, conceding 24 times in 10 games in the main section, while regional conflict badly disrupted preparation.
Switzerland: Yakin is aiming for the 'best World Cup from a Swiss team' as he seeks to turn reliable regulars into contenders this summer. Read the team guide here.
Comfortable in qualifying, topped their group with a mix of experience and fresh talent knitted together by Xhaka.
Some tactical uncertainty over formation, and big expectations from fans despite their side lacking depth beyond the starting XI.
Brazil: Five-time champions have turned to Ancelotti, who has built an attacking side eager to end years of underachievement. Read the team guide here.
Built around Vinícius, the team has a solid spine which allows room for attacking flair in an aggressive 4-2-4 formation.
The full-backs do not match up to former greats, while 34-year-old Neymar may struggle to contribute fully due to injuries.
Haiti: Grenadiers will be group outsiders after reaching their first World Cup since 1974 despite turmoil at home. Read the team guide here.
Migné has built a disciplined side with the pace and skill to counter effectively, with Bellegarde and Isidor bringing proven quality.
Instability has affected the team’s buildup, with key striker Nazon held up in Iran and Migné unable to visit the country he coaches.
Morocco: Atlas Lions made history as Africa’s first semi-finalists in Qatar and expect to make a similar impact after a recent coaching change. Read the team guide here.
Ouahbi’s setup will create space for star player Hakimi, while reaching the last four in 2022 has boosted collective belief.
The Afcon hosts struggled to cope under pressure, culminating in a farcical final, and will be under close scrutiny again this summer.
Scotland: Clarke’s side ended 28-year wait to qualify in cathartic style and will seek to reward travelling fans with a first trip to the knockouts. Read the team guide here.
Built around key lieutenants like McTominay and Robertson, Scotland’s first-choice XI is organised and hugely experienced.
The team lacks a reliable scorer, with Clarke often criticised for his caution, while Billy Gilmour’s injury will hurt a squad lacking depth.
Australia: At their sixth successive finals, the Socceroos arrive with an experienced core, young attacking talent and designs on a first knockout win. Read the team guide here.
Popovic improved the team in qualifying and has made them tougher to beat, while Irankunda leads a dangerous counterattacking unit.
The new coach is eager to shake off the ‘underdogs’ tag, but it may prove tough with a lack of high-profile names in a transitional squad.
Paraguay: Alfaro has rebuilt the team around 'Paraguayan DNA – intensity and clean sheets' and hopes of progress are high after 12 years away. Read the team guide here.
La Albirroja will rely on the assets that saw them through qualifying: playing a physical style with the tenacity to dig out unlikely results.
Only two teams scored fewer goals in Conmebol qualifying and there may be an over-reliance on Enciso to create and take chances.
Türkiye: After a remarkable 22-year absence following their third-place finish in 2002, Montella's talented squad are primed to make an impact on their return to the world stage. Read the team guide here.
Montella has built a harmonious squad with in-form players and two of Europe’s brightest attacking talents in the shape of Guler and Yildiz.
Lack of a proven striker and big-game experience in some areas increases the risk of the wheels coming off as they did at Euro 2020.
USA: Expectations are low for the co-hosts after a turbulent buildup, but there is a path to the latter stages if Pochettino can harness his team’s abilities. Read the team guide here.
The core of the squad are ‘glue guys’ with prior World Cup experience, while their head coach knows how to win knockout matches.
Pochettino still seems unclear on his best team and tactical setup, leaving many home fans frustrated before a ball has been kicked.
Ecuador: At their fifth World Cup, this may be El Tri’s strongest squad, seeking to win their first knockout game after qualifying in impressive fashion. Read the team guide here.
A defence marshalled by Pacho and Hincapié conceded just five goals in 18 qualifiers and Beccacece has introduced a Bielsa-esque pressing mentality.
Scoring remains a problem and beyond veteran striker Enner Valencia, attacking options are talented but raw and unproven at the highest level.
Germany: Winners in 2014, Die Mannschaft crashed out at the group stage in the last two finals but have rebuilt well under tactical obsessive Nagelsmann. Read the team guide here.
A blend of rising stars and reliable stalwarts, this squad has more than enough creative talent to take advantage of a decent group-stage draw.
This is not yet a vintage Germany side and results have been inconsistent, while Neuer is back in goal after a reliable successor could not be found.
Cote D'Voire: The Elephants believe they can do what their golden generation failed to: reach the knockout stages, or as Faé has said: ‘Why not win it?’ Read the team guide here.
Faé’s defence is settled but still flexible and did not concede in qualifying, and the coach has a wealth of attacking talent at his disposal.
There are questions over midfield selection and their underwhelming Afcon defence has lowered previously high expectations this summer.
Japan:
Perennial dark horses capable of causing shocks, impressive warm-up results have fuelled belief they can break new ground by reaching the quarter-finals.
 Read the team guide here.
Samurai Blue play as a cohesive unit, pressing from the front in Moriyasu’s settled system, and now have the squad depth to make a deeper run.
Injury to Kaoru Mitoma is a blow and they have landed in a tough group with three experienced and physical opponents.
Netherlands:
Koeman has been set a target of reaching the semi-finals, but has been forced to prioritise strength and fitness over skill with a raft of injury issues.
 Read the team guide here.
The Oranje smashed in 27 goals to qualify unbeaten, but it is their back four which looks most impressive on paper, marshalled by captain Van Dijk.
Several key players have suffered from injury layoffs or lack of game time this season, and facing Japan first will test this team’s cohesion.
Sweden: Took two points from 18 in a disastrous qualifying campaign, but grasped their playoff chance under Potter and have the attacking talent to go further. Read the team guide here.
Potter has two elite finishers at his disposal up front but will set up with a hard-working back five to complement the firepower in his squad.
Isak endured a grim first season at Liverpool, and Potter has had limited time to apply his methods after taking over last October.
Tunisia: After six World Cups and six group-stage exits, the Eagles of Carthage seek to break new ground with an imposing team drawn from the country’s diaspora. Read the team guide here.
Did not concede a goal in qualifying and have been tactically flexible under Lamouchi, who has pleased supporters with his desire to bring young talent through.
Burnley’s Mejbri is the creative star of a low-key team lacking elite experience, who may find it difficult to play with freedom in a challenging group.
Belgium: A time of transition for the Red Devils. Qualifying went smoothly but was never particularly eye-catching.  Read the team guide here.
De Bruyne, Doku and Lukaku offer a serious attacking edge, though the latter played only 64 minutes for Napoli this season.
The defence is, except for Courtois, the weak point with the golden generation of Alderweireld, Kompany, Vermaelen and Vertonghen long gone.
Egypt: Salah led the way through qualifying but limitations of the side were exposed at Afcon, where Senegal inflicted a semi-final defeat. Read the team guide here.
Cohesive, often hard to score against and emotionally committed.
Can look blunt if opponents double up on Salah and the midfield cannot pass through the press.
Iran: Smooth sailing in qualifying – anything but easy since then. The conflict with the United States threw their involvement into doubt but Ghalenoei's side are all set to compete. Read the team guide here.
Capable of mixing things up – in March friendlies they played a 3-6-1 against Nigeria and a 4-4-2 against Costa Rica.
Ghalenoei and his staff will have to work hard to minimise disruption for the squad, which will be based in Mexico but will play three group games in the US.
New Zealand: The All Whites are the lowest-ranked team at the tournament but the squad has evolved from part-timers to professionals. Read the team guide here.
There's no shortage of optimism – within the camp there's belief they can to make the knockout rounds for the first time.
Star striker Wood has had an injury-plagued 2026 and recent friendly results have been mixed at best.
Cabo Verde: An eclectic group of players, the Blue Sharks are swimming in completely uncharted waters as they make their World Cup debut. Read the team guide here.
A settled squad has been together for the best part of half a decade. Physical and happy to defend but blessed with technical forwards too.
Key defender Logan Costa has been out with an anterior cruciate ligament injury all season
Saudi Arabia: The Green Falcons have had a chaotic buildup to the tournament, with Donis taking charge in April after the bitter exit of Hervé Renard. Read the team guide here.
Expectations are low, so to some extent the pressure is off. Expect Donis to focus his efforts on defensive solidity.
The team looks toothless up front: just seven goals were scored in 10 games in the main round of qualification.
Spain: Rightly among the favourites. De la Fuente has the perfect blend of youth and experience, prodigious talent and maturity. Read the team guide here.
Lamine Yamal and Williams have injected freshness into a team that still dominates the ball. The frontline will be hard to contain.
Are there any? The back four can have its moments but this is simply a fiercely competitive and united team.
Uruguay: The quarter-finals are the aim, but the buildup has been anything but smooth. Bielsa has been under pressure since a 5-1 loss to the USA in November. Read the team guide here.
Brace yourselves for Bielsa-ball: expect La Celeste to press their opponents high up the field and chase the ball at all times.
Uruguay do not have the scoring power of old. Hopes are being pinned on Darwin Núñez, who has struggled for form at Al-Hilal.
France: France have attacking talents that are the envy of the world. But will Deschamps take the handbrake off and let them shine? Read the team guide here.
The front four is a remarkable quartet, and the back four isn't bad either. Their bench might be the strongest at the tournament.
A cynic might suggest the head coach's conservatism. More accurately, it's the challenge he faces in putting all the puzzle pieces together.
Iraq: After a marathon journey to get here (they played 21 qualifiers, more than anyone else) Arnold's side are out to prove they belong on the world stage. Read the team guide here.
As Arnold says, the pressure is on the other three teams in the group. Iraq have nothing to lose.
Not exactly free-scoring. Breaking down three tough defences in the group will be a huge challenge.
Norway: Golden generation vibes for Haaland and friends. But expect Solbakken's side to prioritise effectiveness over aesthetics. Read the team guide here.
Haaland will be eager to grab this opportunity on the world stage. The team averaged nearly five goals a game in qualifying.
Tough group means they have to hit the ground running. First-choice goalkeeper has barely played for his club this season.
Senegal: The Lions of Teranga arrive in North America in fine shape, thanks to a freshened-up frontline and a defence that is its usual sturdy self.  Read the team guide here.
Thiaw has developed a more flexible tactical approach, while speed in attack will cause teams plenty of problems.
Recent tournament record, aside from the most recent Cup of Nations, is unimpressive.
Algeria: One of this World Cup’s great unknowns. Qualifying was a cakewalk – but against generally poor opposition. Read the team guide here.
The squad boasts plenty of technical ability and Afcon highlighted just how good they can be at their best.
The Afcon quarter-final collapse against Nigeria remains fresh in minds. Was it an aberration or a sign of how this team performs under pressure?
Argentina: World Cup and Copa América holders travel with a squad of familiar faces but perhaps not with players in peak physical condition. Read the team guide here.
Almost all of the class of 2022 is still around, including Messi.
Several players had injury setbacks at the end of very demanding seasons with their clubs.
Austria: Rangnick's high-pressing unit know exactly who they are. This is a side built not on stardom but on familiarity, trust and collective movement. Read the team guide here.
Continuity: Austria’s plan has been remarkably stable for years. Rangnick has had time to imprint his ideas.
If the structure slips even slightly, the aggressive counter-pressing approach can leave them exposed. Pre-tournament injury to Christoph Baumgartner is a huge blow.
Jordan: A first finals appearance for a team who qualified with a match to spare. Will likely sit deep in a back five.  Read the team guide here.
Will look to exploit quick transitions and the pace of star winger Mousa Al-Taamari.
Injury has ruled out key striker Yazan A-Naimat, leaving a huge hole in attack. Big-game experience is in short supply.
Colombia: Experienced squad endured a rollercoaster qualifying campaign, beating Brazil and Argentina but losing to a poor Bolivia side. Read the team guide here.
Goals shouldn't be a problem. Suárez is coming off a prolific season in Portugal with Sporting and only Argentina scored more in Conmebol qualifying.
Tournament football leaves no room for the inconsistency that has become a hallmark of this side.
DR Congo: Pragmatic, detail-obsessed coach has the Leopards purring, with a united squad built around a clear collective identity. Read the team guide here.
Extremely difficult to break down and mentally tough as they come. Resilience defined their qualification campaign.
Rarely dominate games and struggle to create freely in open play. Preparations have been disrupted by Ebola outbreak in country.
Portugal: One last hurrah for Ronaldo but last year's Nations League winners have quality throughout and lofty ambitions. Read the team guide here.
The core of the team is settled and the options varied and versatile. A squad still mourning Diogo Jota have a personal, collective mission.
Few and far between but there's always a risk of Ronaldo's outsized influence becoming a problem.
Uzbekistan: A historic first World Cup beckons. Cannavaro has stuck with the 5-2-3 system that powered the White Wolves through qualifying. Read the team guide here.
Qualification was built off a solid defence that includes Khusanov, with just seven goals conceded in 10 games.
Cannavaro was a legend as a player but his managerial career has been mixed. Goals are likely to be a problem.
Croatia: Semi-finalists in 2018 and 2022. Likely to revert to a back four after recent wing-back experiment brought mixed results. Read the team guide here.
Bags of experience and, as past World Cups have shown, a winning mentality. Modric remains a midfield maestro.
Can the old guard still cut it? All that experience means plenty of miles in the legs and sapping temperatures ahead.
England: Cruised through qualifying but the opposition was hardly taxing. So it's the usual question: how will they fare when they come up against the best in a knockout tie? Read the team guide here.
They have enviable attacking options, a host of No 10s and in Rice one of the best midfielders in the world.
There are question marks over the defensive options and, as ever, fitness concerns over key players.
Ghana: A team littered with attacking talent that cruised through qualifying but their recent run of defeats is a concern. Read the team guide here.
Have developed into a major threat from set pieces and in Semenyo the Black Stars have one of the most in-form attackers in European club football.
Lack of elite defenders is a worry and goalkeeping unit lacks international experience.
Panama: La Marea Roja are hopeful of improving upon hapless 2018 showing after long development under former Leeds coach. Read the team guide here.
Squad has been together a long time, has pace and is full of confidence. Solid recent showings in Gold Cup and Nations League.
Tend to struggle against the bigger teams and several key players are now well into their 30s.

A favourite in the Czechia national team after the few days in the spring when he helped seal two playoff successes via penalty shootouts. Before then he had only saved one spot-kick in domestic football, but he excelled in the scrap for a World Cup spot like nobody else in the Czech squad. “It feels like a dream,” he said after the wins over the Republic of Ireland and Denmark. Kovar is a huge talent, calm by nature and mostly phlegmatic. As a teenager, he left a small Czech town to join Manchester United. He has since won three league titles in three different countries: Czechia, Germany and the Netherlands. Although he’s usually quiet and modest, he thrives in the big moments and coaches joke that he brings luck. “It wasn’t any great luck, I simply did my homework,” he said while the whole country was lauding him. Still, speculation persists over whether he will be the first-choice goalkeeper for the World Cup.

Zima can come across as a rather unusual young man, especially in his public appearances. At first glance, you cannot tell what kind of day he’s having. After the first question, you still don’t know how the interview will go. Zima – meaning “winter” – is not a flashy star, despite the fact his career quickly took off as a teenager. At 19, with just 156 minutes in the domestic league, he was signed by Slavia Prague from Sigma Olomouc for more than €1m, a fee rarely seen in Czech football for such a player. The move did not faze him. “I have no reason to be nervous,” he said. “The pitch is always the same size. Opponents don’t scare me.” A year and a half later, he moved to Italy for four times that fee, joining Torino. In January 2024, he returned to Slavia Prague to restart his career and, at €4m, became the most expensive signing in Czech league history. Now a four-time domestic league champion, he is widely praised for his precise approach to defending, though critics still say he can be too laid-back, and prone to defensive lapses.

Fans of human anatomy should take a look at Tomas: the centre-back has what may well be the biggest calves at the tournament. He’s not particularly tall, but is pure muscle. He’s also one of the most experienced players in the Czechia squad and is a quiet leader at Slavia Prague, where he has won four league titles, the latest as captain. He comes from a region where cross-country skiing is more common than football but fell in love with the game competing with his two brothers. With no proper pitch in his village, he used to cycle three miles to training. Through consistency and hard work, Holes has gradually developed into a leader without ever acting like a superstar. Despite Czechia being a largely secular country, he is a devout evangelical Christian and says: “Faith is the most important thing for me, apart from my family. I often feel like guardian angels help me on the pitch.” Away from the pitch, Holes enjoys the quiet life with his two daughters, often going fishing and reading history books before bed.

Hranac grew up in a small town in western Czechia, far from major academies – so when his talent became clear, that had to change. At 14, he travelled 60 miles to a boarding school in Plzen while his parents worked across the border in Germany. The sacrifices paid off. These days he has a calm and reserved exterior, and can appear shy, but that disguises the real fight and passion inside him. "Robin takes a lot of hits but never reacts or gets angry,” says his dad. “He has an extremely high pain threshold.” After just one impressive season in the Czech league he broke into the national team, marked Cristiano Ronaldo at Euro 2024, and earned an €8m move to Hoffenheim in 2024. Best deployed in the middle of a back three.

Long overlooked due to his slight build, Coufal was told at 17 by coaches at the Czech club Banik Ostrava that he would never make a living from football. He was quick and determined, but too small and easily outmuscled in duels. At that time, he hated football. “But I promised myself I’d prove them all wrong. I’m a bit of a madman who likes chasing his dreams,” he said. True recognition only came at 26, when he was signed by Slavia Prague and he went on to win three consecutive league titles before making a surprise move to the Premier League. “At first I thought they had the wrong name. Why would they sign a veteran?” he joked of his move to West Ham. In London he enjoyed a fairytale spell, culminating in winning the Europa Conference League. But after five years he found himself on the periphery with the Hammers. Again, though, he refused to give up. Now 33, he has rebuilt his career at Hoffenheim and is playing arguably his best football.

One of the breakout stars of the recent Czech league season, one of the country’s best out-and-out defenders and a champion with Slavia, Chaloupek’s performances were such that he attracted interest from Roma and Fiorentina in January. A year earlier, however, he wasn’t even in the starting lineup after a tough time with injury. He’s a hard-working, disciplined and reliable defender – a nightmare for attackers due to his uncompromising style. Off the pitch, he is quiet and reserved. Had football not worked out, he says he might have become a police officer. “I liked the idea of being fair, principled and standing up for the truth,” he says. Chaloupek was born with a cleft palate and underwent surgery at the age of three. “I was mocked by other kids because of it. It was hard, but it made me stronger.” He later considered plastic surgery as he still breathes through only one nostril.

Krejci’s childhood dream of playing in the Premier League turned into something of a nightmare last season as Wolves endured defeat after defeat, suffering relegation to the Championship. The centre-back, however, quickly – and to the surprise of some – turned into one of Rob Edwards’ most valuable players. Over the past four years, his rise has been rapid. He won two league titles with Sparta Prague, became the most expensive signing in Girona’s history, before a loan to the Premier League last summer. Krejci follows a simple motto: ”If you feel you should do, decide or change something, don’t hesitate. No one else will do it for you.” He used to struggle with discipline and picked up too many yellow cards. Yet since March, he has been captain of the national team and led with distinction, scoring in the playoff games against the Republic of Ireland and Denmark. “I believed in myself because I know what I can do,” said the 27-year-old.

An unassuming character, when Darida played for Freiburg from 2013 to 2015 he rode a scooter to training. He got rid of it when he moved to Berlin with Hertha, though. “It wasn’t really safe in Berlin traffic,” he said. “My father took it back to Czechia and I gave it to my sister.” It wasn’t an easy journey into professional football: he almost had to quit the game when he was 16 when his growth stopped, leaving him struggling to handle the physicality of the game. But, via hard work and a gluten-free diet, he developed the strength needed. He spent seven years at Hertha before moving to Aris in Greece in 2022, and returning to Czechia last year with Hradec Kralove. He brings huge experience, having made his international debut back in 2012, and captained the team at Euro 2020. After that tournament he retired from international football, saying: “I experienced beautiful moments in the national team, but now, I’d like to spend much more time with my family and my young son.” But he was tempted back in March this year, returning, aged 35, to help them in the World Cup qualification playoffs.

A real talent, who could make a big impact. Hlozek has played in Germany since 2022 when Bayer Leverkusen took note of his record at Sparta Prague: a senior debut at 16, scoring 40 goals and making 36 assists in 132 games, and winning the Czech Cup. He joined for an initial €13m, but stayed for only two years, having grown frustrated with a rotational role, moving to Hoffenheim for an initial €17m. Hugely versatile, he’s a threat out wide or through the middle. He’s a big fan of tattoos, with a giant lion on his left thigh. “It has a deep, personal meaning for me and gives me strength,” he said last year. “Leo is my star sign and I identify with the animal. The lion is known for its fighting mentality, exudes an aura and is the king of the wilderness. It took five and a half hours in the first sitting, then we took a break and after that it was another five and a half hours. But I'm happy that I got through it. I like it a lot."

Schick’s goalscoring gift was obvious from a very young age. Playing for Vestec, a village near Prague, he didn’t celebrate his goals, said coaches, but would instead just pick the ball up, take it to the centre circle and ask for the game to be resumed. When he missed a big chance, he would cry and had to be substituted. Aged eight he was inspired by watching Wayne Rooney play for Manchester United at Sparta Prague. He recalled: “I thought that I want to do this – never get a normal job, and earn a living like him.” It worked out well. He played a grand total of 36 league minutes in Sparta Prague’s first team before Sampdoria decided they had seen enough, paying €4m for the gangly 20-year-old. He signed for Roma a year later in a move that could have been worth up to a club record €42m, but it didn’t really work out there: he ended up on the wing, was loaned to Leipzig, then in 2020 was sold for €26.5m to Leverkusen – which is where everything clicked. In April this year, he scored his 100th goal for them in all competitions. He helped Czechia qualify for the first time in 20 years via the playoffs. He was 10 when they last played at a World Cup. “I vividly remember the games. The Czech fans have waited a long time for this.”

An experienced forward who made his senior debut for Slavia Prague back in 2016, and now, a decade later, turns out for their rivals Sparta. Kuchta also had spells in Russia with Lokomotiv Moscow and Denmark with Midtjylland. Life with the international side hasn’t always been easy: in November 2023 he was one of three players – with Jakub Brabec and Vladimir Coufal – kicked out of the training camp for going clubbing two days before a Euro 2024 qualifier against Moldova. Aggressive and powerful on the pitch, he’s more nurturing off it, raising chickens, rabbits, ducks and geese at his family farm. When he moved to Moscow in 2022 and had to leave them behind he said: "Chickens are part of my life, I was used to going to them in the morning, then again after training, it cleared my head. It will take a while to adjust. I can’t take them there, it’s -17 degrees … The chickens will just have to wait until I am home, and I will pay a lot of attention to them again."

A cousin of his teammate David Doudera, Cerv made his international debut two years ago, soon after joining Viktoria Plzen from Slovan Liberec, and was the only newcomer in the national side’s Euro 2024 squad. He wasn’t expecting the call when it came. “I didn’t really believe it at first,” he said after arriving at the team’s training camp. “I went on vacation, so when I got the call I had to ​​leave my family there and fly away. I left them there to enjoy the warmth and sunshine. And here we are in the rain and fog. But it's really incredible." Settling in as part of the national setup wasn’t too hard, though: “I know a lot of guys from the under-21s and I have Doudis [Doudera], my cousin, and the guys from Plzen here, so everything is fine. But I'm probably hanging out with Doudis most.” Two years on and he’s fully integrated, and an experienced, reliable option for this World Cup squad. His surname translates as “worm”.

A tall, experienced option up front, Chytil made quite a splash on his international debut in 2022 – scoring a 10-minute hat-trick in a friendly against the Faroe Islands. He’s known for being physical and fearless, a real handful, and could be an important weapon this summer. He spent most of his early career at Sigma Olomouc before 2023’s move to Slavia Prague where, again, he had a scoring debut, netting against Hradec Kralove on the opening day. The club’s manager, Jindrich Trpisovsky, described him well: “The first thing that comes to mind about Mojmir is the wider benefit he brings to the team: his fighting spirit, his annoyingness for defenders. He has very good ball coverage, perhaps the best back-to-goal game in the league. He is a team player, combative, with excellent physical qualities.”

When Jurasek moved from Slavia Prague to Benfica for €14m three years ago, becoming one of the Czech league’s most expensive exports, it seemed Czech football would finally have a full-back at a top European club. His father even flew to Portugal by private jet for the signing ceremony, as Benfica set his release clause at a whopping €80m, an indication of the regard in which they held him. However, a serious ankle injury disrupted his progress, and he lost his place in the Benfica first team. Jurasek rebuilt his career during a loan spell at Hoffenheim, before returning to Slavia in January. “I just hope I don’t bring bad luck,” he confessed before helping them to the league title – the first title success of his career. With a strong left foot, excellent stamina and acceleration, a big physical presence and a great crossing ability, Jurasek has just about every attribute you would want from a left-back.

Widely linked with a big move after this tournament – this summer is a real chance for Sulc to showcase his talents. Soon after being voted the best Czech player of 2025 he joined Lyon from Viktoria Plzen for an initial €7.5m, handed the formidable task of filling the void left behind by Rayan Cherki. But he shrugged off that pressure and stepped up with some superb displays, earning plenty of praise from supporters. The reception surprised him. “It’s been incredible,” he said in April. “Honestly, I didn't expect so much love from fans or that it would happen so quickly … It’s my first experience in one of the top five leagues in Europe, and the football in Czechia is simply much less demanding. The coach has been brilliant with me.” He’s happy to be versatile, too. “I'll always do my best, even if they put me as a centre-back!”

Stanek has never got anything for free in his career. He started out as an ice hockey player and was a promising forward, a talent he inherited from his father. But he chose to leave the ice in pursuit of a football career and went straight from Sparta to England, where he was a backup goalkeeper at Everton, facing shots from Romelu Lukaku, Kevin Mirallas and Samuel Eto’o in training. “I felt like I was in another world. I was taking a battering, but I didn’t want to give up,” he later recalled. He dreamed of following in the footsteps of his compatriot Petr Cech, but had to take the long way round. He even spent a season in the Czech third division to build his confidence. ”In hindsight, I feel like a cat with seven lives,” he said of his nomadic career. “That’s why when I go to the zoo, I spend most of my time with the tigers. I look for inspiration in them.” He eventually settled with Viktoria Plzen, where his career took off, leading to a move to Slavia Prague in 2024.

An imposing 1.88m (6ft 2in) presence out wide, he is pacy as well. Provod rose through the ranks at his hometown club, Viktoria Plzen, then had a series of loans as he established himself, first at Banik Sokolov, then Ceske Budejovice and finally Slavia Prague, whom he joined on a permanent deal in 2020. “It feels unbelievable,” he said when he signed, “it feels like a beautiful story. It all happened really fast. It’s a great challenge for me, and I did not hesitate. Slavia is the biggest and most successful club in Czechia, so it was clear immediately.” He made his international debut the same year in a Nations League game against Slovakia. He missed Euro 2020 because of injury, but made the squad for 2024 and scored in the opener against Portugal. A versatile performer, he could also be called upon to do a job more centrally, or up front.

At 16, Sadilek made a bold move. Instead of following his older brother Lukas through the academy system in his home country, he left for the Netherlands, joining PSV. Maybe the time apart did them good. “As kids we were together every day,” remembered Michal, “and sometimes like all little boys we got on each other's nerves, fought and the like.” But these days they couldn’t be closer. “I’m proud of my brother. We write to each other after every match, and when there's a chance, we talk about everything.” He moved to Twente in 2022 for three years, before returning home with Slavia in 2025. His international career hasn’t been without its ups and downs: he made his debut in 2021 but had to pull out of the Euro 2024 squad after injuring his leg when he fell off his tricycle at the training camp. The FA said the incident happened when he drove the three-wheeled bike through a pothole and crashed, but it did not criticise him. “The accident happened in the player's free time, which he was allowed to spend as he pleased. He did not violate team rules or other internal agreements."

A 1.98m (6ft 6in) powerhouse who isn’t afraid of getting stuck in. In January he embraced his bad-boy image, saying: “People don’t like me? That actually makes me feel good.” But in May things reached a tipping point: he was sent off for elbowing an opponent in the head in a chaotic Prague derby, his third red of the season, prompting Slavia’s furious chair, Jaroslav Tvrdik, to transfer-list him. “Tomas is clearly unable to control his behaviour,” said Tvrdik. “With this behaviour, he does not belong on the field.” The league’s disciplinary committee banned him for six games, saying the elbow was “not an accidental event … neither emotions nor the assertive style of play that Tomas Chory presents can be an excuse for such an action”. He has plenty of experience, and has spent his whole club career in Czechia apart from a loan spell in Belgium with Zulte Waregem. He made his international debut in 2023, scoring and assisting in a 3-0 Euro 2024 qualifying win over Moldova.

One of the select few footballers who fans have forgiven for playing for both rival Prague clubs. An easy-going character, Zeleny is in no way a rebel or troublemaker, but he can be impatient, particularly when driving his car. “It annoys me when someone dawdles at the lights because they are on their phone,” he says. “That’s when I lean on the horn. Otherwise, I’m calm. People say you need to be ruthless in top football, but it’s not in my nature.” Zeleny is unlikely to change his nature now as he approaches his 34th birthday. He has never left the Czech league, making over 300 appearances since his debut for Hradec Kralove in 2010. Earlier in his career, he may have lacked the courage to move abroad; now he’s nearing the end of his time as an evergreen of Czech football. Fittingly, his surname translates to “green” in English.

Like his Slavia teammate Tomas Chory, Doudera had a lively Prague derby in May, with both shown red cards as the game descended into a mess of crowd violence. Doudera’s red was for abusing the referee; Slavia’s chair, Jaroslav Tvrdik, responded by transfer-listing him. The defender later apologised, writing online: "I'm sorry for the whole situation. To the fans, to the whole of Slavia, to Czech football. These things shouldn't happen in a civilised world.” He now has a chance to redeem himself this summer. He made his international debut in 2023, a year after his move to Slavia. He said soon afterwards: “My dad and I always say that my story is worth a book. But I don't want to brag about it, it's just that I have it in me. Each of us has a story and everyone got here somehow. I wasn't a great talent from a young age. I was never in the youth national teams … I'm proud of myself for what I've accomplished.” Teammate Lukas Cerv is his cousin.

It wasn’t an easy season for Soucek as West Ham struggled, but he remains a fundamental part of Miroslav Koubek’s national side – a brilliantly energetic 1.93m (6ft 4in) force in midfield. Last year he was named Czech footballer of the year for the fourth time. He was brought up in Havlickuv Brod, a town with a population of 23,000 people, and comes from a sporting family: his dad a football coach and his mum a runner. “She runs half-marathons and marathons and sometimes when I was younger I went with her to the forest,” he says. “And sometimes when I was in pre-season I would go with her to run in the forest. I think I got my stamina from her.” Last year he published his autobiography, in which he revealed he had considered retiring early during what were “two years of horror” spent with insomnia and depression. He improved with medical help, and said his trademark “helicopter” goal celebration rose from the experience: “From match to match, I focused mainly on not sleeping, which actually disturbed me doubly. And that’s why the helicopter was created, my goal celebration. I start to spin slightly and enjoy the feeling of taking off. I like it when fans call me a helicopter. It’s a symbol of what I’ve done, what I’ve overcome, and where I am. It expresses my inner feeling that I can fight.”

Hornicek has spent roughly a third of his life in Portugal, where he moved aged 17. He was based in a boarding school 1,500 miles from home and was homesick, but never gave up his dream of a career in football. “That decision took away part of the youth I could have spent with friends, but I followed my dream. Even if I could turn back time, I wouldn’t change it,” he says. Nicknamed “Horny Czech“ in Portugal because of the difficulty of pronouncing his surname, he’s now a rising star in Czech goalkeeping. He started in Braga’s youth team and spent two years as a backup, before a spectacular breakthrough last season. He kept a clean sheet every other match and became known for saving penalties in the Europa League. Boasting high levels of concentration, he has improved his distribution and work on the ball in Portugal and has even been linked with Real Madrid of late. “It’s a shame my grandfather didn’t live to see [this]. He was my biggest supporter,” he says.

Raised in a footballing family. Sojka’s dad, Jindrich, was chair of SK Klatovy for more than 20 years, and his older brother plays for them now. Alexandr has gone the furthest in the family, though. He returned to his first club, Viktoria Plzen, this year when they activated a buy-back clause, re-signing him from Hradec Kralove. “We decided to activate the option," said the club’s sporting director, Martin Vozábal. "The goal is to increase competition in midfield and he performed very well during the autumn.” He has proved himself as a technically gifted, versatile performer. His international inclusion was an overwhelming moment for his dad. "The whole family lives for it,” Jindrich told iSport. “The only pity is that his grandfather, a big fan of Plzen since childhood, did not live to see it. Sasa [Alexandr] is finally showing what is in him. People in this region live for football and they appreciate that a boy from Klatovy can reach such a level."

The baby of the squad, Sochurek was still 17 when the final selection was announced. A product of Sparta’s academy, he made his club debut last year, and his international debut in a warm-up game against Kosovo in May. But his cool, fearless approach convinced the coach, Miroslav Koubek, he was ready. After his first-team breakthrough at Sparta, their coach, Brian Priske, said: “He plays like he's over 30. The first-team players immediately took him in and when they saw what he could do with the ball.” Sochurek’s youth coach Pavel Drsek told Eurofotbal.cz in May: “He's made a huge improvement in the last year, he’s grown bigger, he has strong thighs, it's hard to get him off the ball. He’s not a typical Czech midfielder, he likes the ball, his first thought is to go forward … And he's a great guy, a pure soul, but quiet. Once I handed him the captain's armband before a match and he immediately told me that he could not be the captain. He is not a classic leader, but he is clearly a driving force.”

A promising young winger who knew what he wanted from the moment he first kicked a ball. “I first played in the village where I was born, for AFK Horin, at the age of three,” he recalled. “Then we moved and I started playing for Melnik. When I was six, we played a tournament somewhere, I don't know where exactly, and Slavia Prague scouted me there. So I went to Slavia for a trial and joined them when I was six.” He made rapid progress, and last year signed for Viktoria Plzen from Slovan Liberec. Viktoria’s sporting director, Daniel Kolar, called him “an extraordinary talent, which he confirmed in the Liberec jersey. Despite his still young age, he has already played almost 80 league matches. We have a clear development plan with him and we intend to push his potential even further.” Technically gifted, he has pace and an eye for goal – a useful option this summer. Models himself on Kevin De Bruyne.
